front.title: The MERKLE3 Incremental Scheme for ZONEMD

abstract.t: The ZONEMD Resource Record affirms the integrity of whole DNS zones and helps verify their authenticity. It embeds a cryptographic hash of the zone data, collated in a configurable way. It is used as a checksum for zone transfers between name servers.

defined a single ZONEMD collation scheme, SIMPLE. It is sufficient for small and infrequently updated zones. This document introduces the MERKLE3 scheme, targeting large, dynamic zones. It uses a Merkle tree to enable parallelism and incremental computation.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: A ZONEMD record is generated with a choice of hash function and collation scheme. For the hash function, choices of SHA-384 and SHA-512 have been defined. The collation scheme decides how the hash function is applied to the zone data. The SIMPLE scheme hashes the concatenation of the records in the zone, in canonical order. With its definition, notes:

blockquote.t: For the SIMPLE scheme, the digest is calculated over the zone as a whole. This means that a change to a single RR in the zone requires iterating over all RRs in the zone to recalculate the digest. SIMPLE is a good choice for zones that are small and/or stable, but it is probably not good for zones that are large and/or dynamic.

section.t: The SIMPLE scheme does not support parallelism or efficient incremental computation. Every change to the zone requires re-hashing all of the zone contents, serially. For DNSSEC signers, computing ZONEMD with the SIMPLE scheme is the only step that cannot be parallelized.

This document describes a new collation scheme targeting large, dynamic zones. It organizes the records in the zone in a Merkle tree structure. Records have fixed positions in the tree, so they are unaffected by additions and removals. Changes to the zone only require re-hashing the affected nodes of the tree and their parents.

Using this scheme, ZONEMD checksums can be computed in a highly-parallel fashion. Given the prevalence of many-core CPUs, an order-of-magnitude speedup is achievable. Implementations can persist the tree structure for incremental computation, with even better speedups.

section.name: Computation
section.t: The MERKLE3 data structure is a trie. It consists of four levels: level 0 (the root node), level 1 (up to 256 nodes), level 2 (up to 65,536 nodes), and level 3 (individual RRsets). The first three levels (0, 1, and 2) are inner nodes. Nodes in levels 0 and 1 have up to 256 children each. Children are identified by an unsigned 8-bit index from 0 to 255.

Every RRset is individually hashed, using the selected ZONEMD hash algorithm. The records in the RRset are sorted in DNSSEC canonical order, serialized in the DNSSEC canonical form, concatenated together, and hashed once. Each RRset is assigned to a level-2 node in the tree, based on the first two bytes of its hash. The first byte selects a node in level 1 and the second selects a node in level 2.
Note: in the incredibly unlikely case that two RRsets have the same hash, they should not be deduplicated: both hashes should be inserted in the tree.

Within each level-2 node, RRsets are sorted lexicographically by their hashes. These hashes are concatenated and hashed, using the same hash algorithm, to produce the hash of the level-2 node. Level-2 nodes that have no children are not hashed at all.

Then, the hashes of the level-1 nodes are computed. The children of each level-1 node (those that exist) are ordered by index. The hashes are concatenated and hashed to produce the hash of the level-1 node. Again, level-1 nodes that have no children are not hashed at all.
The root node is hashed from the level-1 nodes in the same way. The hash of the root node is the final digest that is stored in the ZONEMD record.

section.name: MERKLE3 Scheme Inclusion/Exclusion Rules
section.t: The inclusion and exclusion rules for the MERKLE3 scheme are identical to those for the SIMPLE scheme, described in Section 3.3.1.1 of .

section.name: MERKLE3 Scheme Digest Calculation
section.t: A zone digest using the MERKLE3 scheme is calculated over the Merkle tree in a bottom-up fashion. Each branch node in the tree has its own hash value, which is calculated from the elements directly beneath it.
A leaf node's hash value is directly the RRset hash value and corresponds to the leaf position in the tree.

A branch node (including root) hash value is calculated by concatenating all of its child node hash values, sorted numerically, as input to the zone digest hash function. Note that for branch nodes, their assigned hash value may (in fact, usually will) not correspond to its position in the tree (and the common prefix of leaves' hash values).
The root node hash value becomes the zone digest, placed in the RDATA of the apex ZONEMD RR.
Upon a change to a leaf node, the inner node hash values are recalculated from the bottom up, until reaching the root node.

section.name: Adding an RRset
section.t: To add an RRset to the MERKLE3 data structure (subject to inclusion/exclusion rules), its location is determined as described above. A new leaf node is added with the RRset's hash, and a path of branch nodes up to the tree as well if they don't exist yet.

section.name: Removing an RRset
section.t: To remove an RRset from the MERKLE3 data structure, its location is determined as described above. If the RRset was previously placed in the data structure, its full hash value should have the corresponding leaf node, from which it is then removed. Any branch nodes becoming empty are removed as well.

section.name: Updating an RRset
section.t: Updating an RRset in the MERKLE3 data structure is equivalent to removing the former RRset and then adding the updated RRset.

section.name: Recomputing After Changes
section.t: To recompute the MERKLE3 ZONEMD digest it is only necessary to update all inner hash values along paths from changed leaf nodes back to the root node.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: All security considerations from apply to this specification and the MERKLE3 scheme.

section.name: Performance Considerations
section.t: The MERKLE3 scheme requires an implementation to maintain an in-memory Merkle tree data structure of DNS zone data. This will generally be in addition to an implementation's primary data structure for referencing zone data. As a sample data point, the .SE zone from 2026-02-16 with 8 million records and 1.41 million RRsets required an additional 285 MB of memory in the author's proof-of-concept implementation.

Compared to the SIMPLE scheme (), the time to compute an initial MERKLE3 digest can be larger in a single-threaded application, due to the need to populate the Merkle tree data structure. However, when parallelization and multi-threading are leveraged, the MERKLE3 scheme can perform significantly better.
However, the time to compute updates to the MERKLE3 digest are essentially zero on modern computer systems, whereas the SIMPLE scheme provides no reduction in time for computing updates.

The above considerations apply only to well-balanced Merkle trees. An attacker with the ability to insert RRsets into a zone may be able to intentionally unbalance the MERKLE3 data structure, similar to the Nurgle attack . The performance of the MERKLE3 scheme in such an attack may be degraded at a rate proportional to the fraction of RRsets under the attacker's control. In other words, an attacker would need to control a significant fraction of RRsets in a large zone in order to affect performance.

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: This specification has no impact on user privacy.

section.name: Use of Merkle Tree
section.t: Merkle Tree ensures strong cryptographic properties of the resulting hash while enabling tiny updates to the large structure to be processed in logarithmic time.

A proposed alternative was to simply XOR the hashes of individual RRsets. This would be much simpler to implement, wouldn't need any persistent data structures, would be much faster to compute, and would even allow validating an incremental change without accessing the whole zone. Unfortunately, such a scheme is not cryptographically secure; it could only serve as a checksum against random errors.

section.name: Shape of the Tree
section.t: Several variations of the Merkle tree design were considered, focusing on its height and branching factor (the number of children of a node). There were two main proposals: a radix tree and a static tree.

In the radix tree proposal, inner nodes that have no siblings would be collapsed into their parents. The leaves of the tree (representing individual RRsets) would be located at varying depths from the root. Such a binary tree would have a maximum height of 256, but due to the uniform distribution of nodes by the hash function, the real height would be logarithmic to the number of nodes. It would scale dynamically for the size of the zone while offering logarithmic-time operations.

In the static tree proposal, all leaf nodes would be located at exactly the same height, and all the nodes above them would exist unconditionally. RRsets would be hashed under the leaf nodes. Its operations scale linearly if there are many more RRsets than nodes. There were concerns that a single static tree scheme would not cater to the performance needs of both medium-sized and large zones, that multiple schemes of different configurations would be needed.

These proposals were experimentally implemented with various configurations. They were compared by measuring their runtime performance and memory usage in various scenarios (many tiny zones and one TLD-like large zone):
The single-threaded comptuation times of building the whole tree (non-incremental update) of 8-million RR se. zone were in seconds, respectively:
Binary radix: 9.11, 256-ary Radix: 7.98, 256-ary Static2: 11.43, Static3: 8.03 Static4: 11.11
And the memory consumptions of the persistent Merkle tree were in MiB, respectively:
Binary radix: 616, 256-ary Radix: 369, 256-ary Static2: 279, Static3: 285, Static4: 749

The penultimate option (256-ary static tree, depth 3) proved versatile and almost best in each scenario. It provides good speeds for medium and large zones alike. It was not necessary to define multiple static tree schemes to cover all needs.
Note that the needs for very small zones were not considered, as they are adequately satisfied by the SIMPLE scheme.

section.name: Granularity of hashing
section.t: While the final design operates on units of RRsets, smaller and larger units were considered.

One proposal considered hashing individual resource records (RRs). This would ease the processing of updates: an addition or removal of an RR could be processed without knowledge of the RRset it is contained within. But it would require many more invocations of the hash function (one per RR instead of one per RRset) and would significantly increase the size of the tree.

Another proposal considered hashing whole Nodes (all the RRsets at a particular owner name). This would shrink the Merkle tree, but increase the effort to process an update (significantly more data would have to be hashed to update a single node). Notably, the zone apex, which often contains many RRsets, is affected by every update; this proposal would greatly increase the effort for it.
The accepted proposal, where RRsets are hashed, strikes a balance between hashing too many times and hashing too much. The alternative proposals were not implemented or experimentally evaluated.
